data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The superiority of decentralization is an artifact of observer bias; extreme value statistics ensure that catastrophic shared causes eventually dominate any topology, but the distributed topology hides this by fragmenting the observable failure signal across many isolated operators.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If regulatory or systemic monitoring forces centralized reporting of all small operator failures, the hidden shared causes become visible, and the resilience artifact disappears.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large centralized service actively obfuscates its internal failures or provides opaque status pages, it equally hides its correlated failures, equalizing the observer bias.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In any complex system, heavy-tailed distributions govern catastrophic shared causes. In a centralized system, a total collapse is a single, highly visible event that triggers immediate investigation. In a decentralized network, the same shared cause (e.g., an upstream DNS failure) manifests as many independent, seemingly unrelated outages across different operators. Because the operators are isolated, they do not pool their failure data, and the correlation is never recognized. The decentralized network only appears more resilient because its common-mode failures are censored by the observation framework, not because it possesses superior causal isolation.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
